newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kabila demands Zairean president quit at once.
newsitem.headline: Kabila demands Zairean president quit at once.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Sunday he was demanding the immediate resignation of Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko and assumed Mobutu was preparing to comply.
If Mobutu refused to step down, Kabila's rebel forces have orders to move into the teeming capital Kinshasa, he added.
Kabila was speaking to Reuters in Lubumbashi by telephone from the South African navy vessel Outeniqua, minutes before Mobutu boarded the ship after long delays on both sides.
South African President Nelson Mandela has been on the ship since Friday, trying to bring the two leaders together and spare a bloodbath if the rebels attack Kinshasa.
Kabila said: "I have told President Nelson Mandela that Mobutu would have to resign immediately our talks start otherwise my forces are under instructions to move into Kinshasa should he refuse."
"I am still waiting for Mobutu to board the ship and I can only assume that his delay in arriving is because he is preparing his exit from power," he added.

"I have made it clear that there will be no other item on the agenda other than Mobutu's unconditional resignation. I hope he cooperates otherwise I will leave for home and my forces will move into Kinshasa without delay on Sunday night," he said.
A South African official aboard the ship said on Sunday that negotiators have brokered an agreement in principle for Mobutu to stand down after more than 30 years in power.
"There is an agreement in principle for Mobutu's resignation and the launching of a transitional process," the official, who asked not to be named, told reporters.

Mobutu, who has dominated the sprawling nation at the heart of Africa since seizing power in 1965, wore his distinctive leopard-skin hat as he boarded. Witnesses said he looked grim and sad. He held the hand of his wife Bobi Ladawa with one hand. In the other he held his usual carved walking stick.
But Kabila's forces, after a whirlwind campaign over the last seven months, have taken control of about three quarters of the country. Mobutu's foreign allies have abandoned him.

Asked about Mobutu's fate, Kabila said Mobutu could continue to live in Zaire. "We shall look after him. I am ready to guarantee his safety and that of his family so the man can live in Zaire in peace," he said.
Kabila told Reuters he had protested to Mandela about security on the ship and the fact the rebels had been excluded from the arrangements for the talks.

"I have strongly protested to President Mandela because the security arrangements on the ship are appalling to say the least. The South Africaans had allowed over 100 Zairean security men to board the ship and they also cheated me by flying me to the Congolese port when I had objected," he said.
Kabila says Congo is not a neutral venue and his safety cannot be guaranteed because Congolese President Pascal Lissouba is a close friend of Mobutu.
"I hope no one is thinking of playing any games on board the ship because the consequences would be too hot to contemplate," the rebel leader added.
Shortly after he spoke, his commanders at rebel headquarters in Lubumbashi, Zaire's second largest city, told Reuters that rebel forces were ready to attack the capital.

"There are only two things we are waiting for: the order from General Kabila to attack Kinshasa or to stand down should Mobutu resign," said one rebel commander. "We are ready. We are in position to take Kinshasa."
The commander said the bulk of support units and artillery pieces were now in position for the assault.
Rebel sources had earlier told Reuters the alliance would delay the final push on Kinshasa until it assembled between 10,000 and 12,000 troops near the capital.

A rebel source told Reuters that taking Kinshasa, defended by the ailing president Israeli-trained presidential guard, would only require a few units but a larger force would be needed to hold the sprawling city of about five million.

"Capturing Kinshasa is no problem at all. But a larger force of between 10,000 and 12,000 is being moved to back up the fighting units," the source said. "This is the kind of force needed to stamp rebel authority over Kinshasa."
The rebels said on Saturday they had advanced beyond the town of Kenge and were within 150 km (95 miles) of Kinshasa.
